title: Democrats Debate Iran War Powers as Strikes Test Party Unity
description_short: After U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, Democrats disagreed over a war-powers resolution and Israel policy, creating a test of party unity ahead of 2026 primaries.
description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran tested Democratic unity. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers vote, while Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer opposed the measure and Sen. John Fetterman disputed claims that the attack was illegal. The report also described disagreement over Israel and AIPAC’s role in primaries.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on March 2, 2026, that U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran were testing a Democratic coalition that had largely opposed President Donald Trump’s immigration tactics and criticized his economic policies. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers resolution to constrain the president’s options. The article reported differences within the party: Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer said they would not support the measure, and Sen. John Fetterman rejected arguments that the attack was illegal. It also situated the dispute in a longer debate about Israel and Gaza. AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC had opposed Tom Malinowski after he questioned unconditional aid to Israel; in New Jersey’s special primary, progressive Analilia Mejia defeated him. In Illinois, mayor Daniel Biss criticized AIPAC-aligned groups ahead of another primary. The article presented these developments as a political test, not proof of a lasting party realignment.

title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
description_long: On April 11, 2025, POLITICO reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on a proposal connected to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described gathering as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them in a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. It said Prince’s group, partnering with El Salvador, would handle the logistics and would need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine people’s immigration status. The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; those were claims in the pitch, not legal findings. An administration official expected the proposal to be discussed during Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit. Prince and the White House declined to comment. POLITICO also reported that an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming, which the article described as an indication that Prince’s group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching. The report describes proposed terms and a contractor pitch; it does not report an awarded contract or say the camp or flights began.

title: Lawmakers Question Iran War’s Goals and Endgame as Trump Considers Winding Down Operations, AP Reports

title: Trump Signs DHS Funding Bill Ending the Shutdown
description_short: Trump signed DHS funding legislation that ended the shutdown while excluding ICE and CBP Border Patrol from its appropriations.
description_medium: On April 30, 2026, Donald Trump signed a DHS funding measure that ended the shutdown. It funded most DHS agencies through fiscal year 2026, excluding ICE and CBP Border Patrol from its appropriations; employees of those agencies were then being paid under a prior reconciliation law. The bill provided $48 billion for covered agencies.
description_long:
On April 30, 2026, President Donald Trump signed a bill that funded most Department of Homeland Security operations and ended the agency’s shutdown. The measure provided Fiscal Year 2026 funding for covered DHS agencies, totaling $48 billion, while excluding Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection’s Border Patrol; employees of those agencies were being paid through the previous year’s reconciliation law. It identified funded components including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Transportation Security Administration, Coast Guard, and Secret Service.

The measure also included oversight provisions addressing the administration’s immigration-related policies. It directed DHS to develop a uniform policy making federal law-enforcement personnel clearly identifiable, increased funding for DHS’s Office of Inspector General by $37 million, a 20 percent increase, and provided funding for the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and the Office of the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman. The congressional release said the action would restart federal employees’ paychecks and allow services, including FEMA disaster response and Coast Guard operations, to resume.

title: Eleventh Circuit Holds Boca Raton and Palm Beach County Conversion-Therapy Ordinances Violate the First Amendment
description_short: A divided Eleventh Circuit panel held that conversion-therapy ordinances in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County violated the First Amendment.

It directed employers to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States, and assigned payment verification and implementation roles to the State and Homeland Security departments. description_short: AP reported that courts in nine states had rejected DOJ lawsuits seeking detailed voter-registration data, including Maryland.

description_long: The Associated Press reported on June 23, 2026, that U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking Maryland’s detailed voter-registration records. The Justice Department relied on an opinion from its Office of Legal Counsel asserting a right to the data under federal civil-rights law; Gallagher wrote that the court would not interpret the Civil Rights Act contrary to its text simply because the office advancing that view had adopted it. AP said the records sought included dates of birth, addresses, driver’s-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. It reported that Maryland brought the number of states where courts had rejected similar demands to nine, and that DOJ had sued in 30 states and the District of Columbia. title: Court Orders Trump to Pay $2 Million for Trump Foundation Misuse
description_short: A November 2019 court order required Trump to pay $2 million after misuse of Trump Foundation funds for his political interests.
description_medium: On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced a court order requiring Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for misuse of Trump Foundation assets during the 2016 campaign. Trump admitted misusing charitable funds. Settlements also imposed restrictions on future charitable service and directed the dissolved Foundation’s remaining assets to independent charities.
description_long:
On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that the New York Supreme Court had ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for improperly using charitable assets to advance his political interests during the 2016 presidential primaries. The order formed part of the resolution of the state’s lawsuit against the Trump Foundation and its directors.

Trump admitted personally misusing Foundation funds. The admissions included allowing his campaign to control the timing, amounts and recipients of approximately $2.8 million raised through a January 2016 veterans fundraiser. He also admitted using charitable money to settle obligations of companies he controlled and purchasing a $10,000 portrait with Foundation funds.

The Foundation had agreed to dissolve under court supervision in December 2018. The resolution directed its remaining $1.78 million in assets and Trump’s damages payment to eight independent charities. It required training for the Trump children and imposed restrictions on Trump’s future charitable service, including independent oversight and a five-year reporting requirement if he formed a new charity.

description_short: NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate records not transferred at term’s end; 15 boxes were transported in January 2022.

description_long: During 2021, the National Archives and Records Administration worked with Donald Trump’s representatives to locate presidential records that had not been transferred when his administration ended. In statements issued on February 7 and 8, 2022, NARA explained the sequence leading to the return of 15 boxes from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. A representative informed the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located. NARA then arranged secure transport to Washington, receiving the boxes in mid-January 2022. The agency said these records should have been transferred from the White House at the end of Trump’s administration in January 2021 under the Presidential Records Act. Archivist David Ferriero emphasized that complete presidential records enable public accountability and that NARA pursues records improperly removed or not appropriately transferred. NARA said its officials had not visited or raided Mar-a-Lago to collect these boxes.

title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria Response in Puerto Rico: Visit, Relief Challenges and Later Mortality Estimate
description_short: Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria included a paper-towel distribution at a relief center.
description_medium: After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to residents. He had authorized a Jones Act shipping waiver on September 28. GAO later found staffing, logistics and infrastructure failures slowed FEMA’s response. An August 2018 George Washington University report estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 through February 2018.
description_long: Donald Trump visited Puerto Rico on October 3, 2017, after Hurricane Maria devastated the island in September. Reuters photographed him tossing rolls of paper towels into a crowd of residents affected by the storm at a chapel in San Juan. The visit followed his September 28 authorization of a Jones Act waiver intended to expedite relief supplies. ABC News reported criticism of the pace of aid and of the administration’s earlier failure to waive the shipping restrictions. A September 2018 Government Accountability Office report documented challenges that slowed and complicated FEMA’s response. Successive hurricanes created staffing shortages; the territories’ distance from the mainland complicated deployment of personnel and supplies; and damaged power, communications and local response systems required FEMA to assume duties ordinarily performed by territorial authorities. Separately, George Washington University researchers published a report in August 2018 estimating 2,975 excess deaths associated with Maria between September 2017 and February 2018. Their statistical analysis compared observed mortality with an expected baseline, adjusting for age, sex and migration. The estimate describes deaths associated with the hurricane and its aftermath; it does not assign those deaths to Trump’s visit or quantify the contribution of particular federal decisions.

title: Muslim Ban 2.0 — Executive Order 13780
description_short: Executive Order 13780 imposed temporary entry restrictions on nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions in 2017.
description_medium: On March 6, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his first travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of six countries, with exceptions, and a 120-day refugee pause. Iraq was removed from the covered list. Hawaii and Maryland courts blocked key provisions in separate cases. The Fourth Circuit upheld restrictions on enforcement on constitutional grounds; the Ninth Circuit relied on immigration statutes.
description_long:
On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his January travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to exceptions and discretionary waivers. Iraq was removed from the covered-country list. The restriction applied to specified people outside the United States who lacked valid visas at the dates set out in the order. Lawful permanent residents and dual nationals traveling on passports from non-designated countries were among those exempted. A separate provision directed a 120-day suspension of refugee travel and refugee-status decisions, subject to waivers. The scheduled effective date was March 16.

The litigation proceeded through separate cases. Hawaii issued a temporary restraining order against Sections 2 and 6 on March 15, followed by a preliminary injunction on March 29. Maryland enjoined Section 2(c) on March 16. On May 25, the Fourth Circuit substantially upheld the Maryland injunction based on the plaintiffs’ likely success under the Establishment Clause. On June 12, the Ninth Circuit largely upheld the Hawaii injunction on statutory grounds, while narrowing its scope. On June 26, the Supreme Court partly stayed the injunctions, permitting enforcement against people without a credible claim of a bona fide relationship with a person or entity in the United States.

title: Trump Grants a Full Pardon to Otis Gordon
description_short: The archived White House says Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020.
description_medium: President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020. The White House described Gordon as a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries who mentored at-risk young people after a drug conviction. Senator Tim Scott supported the pardon. The Justice Department lists Gordon’s case in the District of South Carolina among the pardons granted that day.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020. The Justice Department lists the pardon under that date and identifies Gordon’s federal case in the District of South Carolina. Its entry describes the offense as selling, distributing, or dispensing a controlled substance. It records a January 11, 1993 sentence of 85 or 86 months in prison, as amended, followed by 48 months of supervised release. The listing leaves that one-month distinction unresolved.

The White House announcement described Gordon’s conviction as possession with intent to distribute. It said he subsequently became a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries and mentored at-risk youths in his community. The announcement also noted that Gordon led a prayer session at the United States Capitol in 2015 following the shooting at a Bible study in Charleston, South Carolina. Senator Tim Scott supported the pardon and praised Gordon’s work helping young men avoid the difficulties he had faced. The action granted a full pardon; it was not announced as a reduction of an ongoing prison sentence.

description_long: Donald Trump granted Steven Benjamin Floyd a full pardon on January 19, 2021. Floyd had pleaded guilty to one count of bank robbery by extortion. The Justice Department lists his Southern District of Mississippi sentence, imposed January 3, 2008, as 30 months, with the final six months to be served in a halfway house, three years of supervised release, and a $2,500 fine. The White House’s announcement identified Representative Mark Green as a supporter of the pardon. It described Floyd as a Marine who enlisted at 17 and earned a combat action ribbon in Iraq. According to that announcement, Floyd left prison in 2009, later raised a family, and operated a successful car repair business. The administration also cited his assistance in extinguishing fires during unrest and his free car repairs for widows and disabled veterans. Trump thanked him for military service and community involvement. Those were the administration’s stated considerations for granting clemency after his prison term had ended.

title: Trump Granted William E. Henry a Full Pardon on January 19, 2021
description_short: Trump granted William E. “Ed” Henry a full and unconditional pardon for his federal theft-of-government-property conviction on January 19, 2021.
description_medium: Donald Trump granted William E. “Ed” Henry a full and unconditional pardon on January 19, 2021. Henry had pleaded guilty to theft of government property arising from assistance in obtaining improper Medicare reimbursements. He received two years’ probation and a $4,000 fine in May 2019. The White House identified Senator Tommy Tuberville as supporting the pardon.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted William E. Henry, also known as Ed Henry, a full and unconditional pardon. Henry’s conviction concerned assistance in obtaining Medicare reimbursements to which physicians were not entitled. According to federal prosecutors’ account of court documents, Henry owned MyPractice24 and served for part of the relevant period as its chief executive. The company provided chronic care management services under contracts with doctors, who billed Medicare and paid the company a share of the reimbursements. Prosecutors said Henry arranged kickbacks for a physician and staff in return for patient referrals and helped the physician reward patients by waiving required copayments. Henry pleaded guilty to one theft-of-government-property count in January 2019. On May 2, 2019, he was sentenced to two years’ probation and a $4,000 fine. The pardon instrument identifies the Middle District of Alabama conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 641 and also lists a $100 special assessment. The White House identified Senator Tommy Tuberville as a supporter of the pardon.

title: Trump Commuted Mark Shapiro’s 85-Year Prison Sentence to Time Served
description_short: A December 2020 clemency warrant commuted Mark Shapiro’s prison sentence to time served; DOJ lists the fraud convictions and restitution.
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, Trump commuted Mark Shapiro’s prison sentence to time served. The DOJ clemency instrument records an 85-year sentence, three years of supervised release, and $22,075,631 restitution for securities, wire, and mail fraud offenses. The White House cited sentence disparity against plea offers, time served, and support from advocates and victims as its rationale. Those reasons are the administration’s account, not an independent finding that the sentence was unjust.
description_long: On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump commuted Mark Shapiro’s 85-year prison sentence to time served. Shapiro had been convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to commit securities, wire and mail fraud, securities fraud, wire fraud and mail fraud. The October 21, 2010 sentence also included three years of supervised release and $22,075,631 in restitution. The commutation left the unpaid restitution balance, a $500 special assessment, supervised release and other sentence components intact. Federal prosecutors described the Cobalt real estate investment scheme as involving false claims about the companies’ history and property holdings, and concealment of Shapiro’s and Irving Stitsky’s control and prior convictions. The White House argued that Shapiro’s prison sentence was disproportionate to a five-to-seven-year plea offer and said he had served longer than that offer. It cited rehabilitation and support from advocates and some victims. These were the administration’s stated grounds for clemency, rather than a court ruling overturning the fraud convictions.

title: Trump commutes James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served
description_short: Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served on January 19, 2021, retaining five years of supervised release and unpaid financial obligations.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served. Cruz had received 480 months for methamphetamine conspiracy in 2001. The warrant retained five years of supervised release and unpaid financial obligations. The White House cited his work and mentoring in prison and identified supporters including Alice Johnson and Dallas pastor Robert Jeffress.
description_long: Donald Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served on January 19, 2021. Cruz had been convicted in the Western District of Texas of conspiracy to possess more than 500 grams of methamphetamine with intent to distribute. His June 26, 2001 sentence included 480 months in prison, five years of supervised release and a $25,000 fine. The commutation warrant records that he had been in federal custody since June 29, 2000, and was incarcerated at the federal prison in Seagoville, Texas. It identifies April 10, 2034 as his projected release date before clemency. Trump’s grant reduced the prison term while leaving the five-year supervision term, its conditions, unpaid fine balance, $100 special assessment and other sentence components in effect. In announcing clemency, the White House cited Cruz’s work and mentoring of other prisoners. It identified Alice Johnson, pastor Robert Jeffress and lawyer Kelly Shackelford among his supporters. The administration presented those rehabilitation claims as reasons to give him another chance.
